title: Seahorse Dads Get Pregnant. #1 Was Lost in a Museum Drawer
description: Seahorse dads get pregnant, their tails are square, and their heads are stealth weapons. But in October 2026 scientists revealed fish that look exactly like seahorses and aren't, and only seven have ever been found. Here are 5 seahorse secrets, counted down to the strangest. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.
sources: Short, G. & Harasti, D. (2026) Australyichthys sea muppets, Journal of Lost Species — https://doi.org/10.66264/y1ffbcwb via ScienceDaily/The Conversation (29 Oct 2026) https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261029072119.htm (7 specimens, ~65 years, >2,500 km, 50–125 m, A. aegis caught 2006 near Gambier Islands, misfiled in invertebrate collection, ethanol-preserved DNA, no coronet or fused belly plates, body plan evolved at least twice, none collected in nearly two decades)

scenes.say: A seahorse is a fish that swims standing up, and its dad gets pregnant. And that's not even the strangest part.

scenes.label: Not seahorses?
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the thing. Scientists just found fish that look exactly like seahorses. And they're not seahorses at all.

scenes.label: Lost in a drawer
scenes.say: One of them sat in the wrong museum drawer for about twenty years. Nobody noticed. We'll open that drawer at the very end.
So today we're counting down five seahorse secrets, from weird to the one that broke the family tree.

scenes.label: 47+ species
scenes.say: There are at least forty-seven known seahorse species. Every single one is a fish. Yes, a real fish, with gills and fins.
Quick question before we start. Which secret do you think is number one? Lock in your guess, and let's see if you're right.

scenes.label: Slowest fish
scenes.say: Number five. Meet the dwarf seahorse, a tiny fish that lives in seagrass. It's the slowest fish on Earth.

scenes.label: 1.5 m per hour
scenes.say: Guinness World Records lists its top speed at about one and a half meters per hour. Per hour!
Think about that. If you moved that slow, crossing your bedroom would take over two hours. A soccer field? Nearly three days.

scenes.label: Thumb-sized
scenes.say: Its whole body is only about two to two and a half centimeters long. That's shorter than your thumb.

scenes.label: 35 beats a second
scenes.say: So how does it move at all? A tiny fin on its back flutters about thirty-five times every second. Like a hummingbird's wings, but underwater.

scenes.label: Nearly 360° vision
scenes.say: And its eyes move on their own. One can look forward while the other looks back, giving it nearly 360-degree vision.

scenes.label: Up to 3,000 a day
scenes.say: Being slow doesn't make it hungry less. A single seahorse can eat up to three thousand brine shrimp in one day.
Three thousand. For a fish shorter than your thumb. And it has to catch every single one of them itself.
Wait, the slowest fish on the planet eats thousands of fast little animals every day? How does that even work? Hold that thought.

scenes.label: A square tail
scenes.say: Number four is hiding in plain sight. Look at the tail. Almost every animal tail is round. A seahorse tail is square.

scenes.label: About 36 segments
scenes.say: Scientists published this in the journal Science in 2015. The tail has about thirty-six square-shaped segments.
Each segment is made of four L-shaped bony plates at the corners. Like a little box built around the backbone.
Seahorses wrap that tail around seagrass and hold on. So the team asked a simple question. Why square and not round?

scenes.label: Square wins
scenes.say: They 3D-printed a square model and a round model, then crushed them both. The square one won every single crushing test.
When you squeeze it, the plates just slide past each other and soak up the force. A round tail turns into a squashed oval.

scenes.label: Better grip
scenes.say: And square segments touch more of a branch at once, so the grip is better. And after a squeeze, the square shape springs back faster, using very little energy.
But here's the twist. A tail can hold you still. It can't catch food. For that, the seahorse uses its head like a weapon.

scenes.label: The escape artist
scenes.say: Number three. This is a copepod, one of the seahorse's favorite foods. It's tiny, and it's one of the fastest escape artists alive.

scenes.label: 500 body lengths/sec
scenes.say: Researchers say a copepod can dart away at more than five hundred body lengths per second.

scenes.label: 2–3 milliseconds
scenes.say: For a six-foot person, that would be swimming at about two thousand miles per hour. And it can react in two to three milliseconds.
So the slowest fish on Earth hunts one of the fastest prey in the sea. That sounds like a losing game, right?
Nope. In 2013, a team at the University of Texas filmed dwarf seahorses with high-speed 3D holography.

scenes.label: A no-wake zone
scenes.say: They found the seahorse's long, arched snout slides through the water making almost no wave in front of it. A little no-wake zone.

scenes.label: 1 millimeter away
scenes.say: The copepod can't feel it coming. The seahorse sneaks to about one millimeter away, then snaps its head up.

scenes.label: Under 1 millisecond
scenes.say: That strike takes less than one millisecond. Faster than the copepod can even react.

scenes.label: 90% success
scenes.say: In calm water, seahorses catch their target about ninety percent of the time. The best of any fish the team tested.
Slowest swimmer. Deadliest snout. That's how three thousand shrimp a day works. But number two is the one everyone talks about.

scenes.label: Dad is pregnant
scenes.say: Number two. In seahorses, the dad is the one who gets pregnant. The mom puts her eggs into a pouch on his belly.

scenes.label: Like a placenta
scenes.say: And this isn't just a bag. In 2021, Australian scientists showed the pouch works like a placenta, a bit like a human pregnancy.
They studied the big-belly seahorse. The father's pouch carries food and oxygen to the babies, and takes their waste away.

scenes.label: Up to ~1,000 babies
scenes.say: The pregnancy lasts about thirty days. And then the dad gives birth to up to around a thousand babies.

scenes.label: 5 to 1,500
scenes.say: Depending on the species, a dad can have as few as five babies, or as many as fifteen hundred in one go.

scenes.label: Almost always pregnant
scenes.say: Then here's the wild part. In many species the mom gives him new eggs right after he gives birth. So the dad can be pregnant almost nonstop.
And the couples often dance together. Courtship can last up to nine hours, and many pairs repeat it every single day. Most species are thought to pair up for life.

scenes.label: 10 days
scenes.say: The tiny dwarf seahorse is even faster. Its pregnancy lasts about ten days, with only three to fifty-five babies.
So we've got a fish that swims upright, has a square tail, a stealth head and a pregnant dad. Surely nothing else could look like that?

scenes.label: The family
scenes.say: Well, seahorses have cousins. Seadragons, like this leafy one. Pipefish. Pipehorses. They're all in the same fish family.
A pipefish is basically a seahorse that never stood up. Long, straight and skinny, but with the same kind of snout.
Scientists thought the seahorse shape evolved just once in that family. One lucky experiment. They were wrong.

scenes.label: The drawer
scenes.say: Number one. Remember that museum drawer? In 2006, a dredge pulled up a tiny thumb-sized fish off South Australia.

scenes.label: Wrong drawer
scenes.say: It was scooped up while scientists were collecting shellfish-like animals. So it got filed with invertebrates, animals without a backbone. Wrong drawer.
It looked like a seahorse. Helmet-shaped head, curled tail, snout. But when researchers scanned its skeleton, things got strange.

scenes.label: No crown
scenes.say: Real seahorses have a bony crown on the head and fused plates on the belly. This fish had neither. Its belly bones were built differently.

scenes.label: DNA still readable
scenes.say: And luckily, it had been kept in alcohol, not formalin. That meant scientists could still read its DNA.

scenes.label: Not a seahorse
scenes.say: The DNA said it wasn't a seahorse. It sat on the branch right next to the seahorses. A whole separate group.
Picture finding a new kind of cat, except it turns out it isn't a cat at all. That's how big this is for fish experts.

scenes.label: Sea muppets
scenes.say: In October 2026, researchers named a new genus with three species. Their nickname? Sea muppets.
The helmethead sea muppet. The bullneck sea muppet. And the paradoxical sea muppet. Yes, those are the real common names.

scenes.label: Only 7 ever found
scenes.say: Here's what blew my mind. All three are known from just seven specimens, collected over about sixty-five years.

scenes.label: 50–125 m deep
scenes.say: They came up by accident in nets and dredges, roughly fifty to a hundred and twenty-five meters deep, across more than two thousand five hundred kilometers of coast.
Think about how weird that is. A fish discovered, named and famous, and not one person has ever watched it swim.

scenes.label: Never seen alive
scenes.say: And no one has collected one in nearly twenty years. Nobody has ever seen a sea muppet alive.

scenes.label: Evolved twice
scenes.say: So the seahorse body plan evolved at least twice. Nature built the same strange design two separate times.

scenes.label: 5 spines, not 4
scenes.say: And it's not only muppets. This August, scientists in India named a brand new spiny seahorse with five crown spines instead of four.
It had been mixed up with lookalikes for over a hundred years. Seahorses are still surprising us, right now.
The researchers think the sea muppets are most likely still down there, in a part of the sea we hardly ever visit.

scenes.label: Which one got you?
scenes.say: So which one got you? The pregnant dad, the square tail, or the fish nobody has ever seen alive? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: Only 7 of These Seahorse Lookalikes Were Ever Found
short.description: They look exactly like seahorses, but DNA says they're not. Only seven have ever been found and nobody has seen one alive. Full story on the channel. #seahorse #shorts

scenes.say: Only seven of these fish were ever found. Nobody's seen one alive.
One sat in the wrong museum drawer for about twenty years, filed with animals that don't even have a backbone.
It looks exactly like a seahorse. Curled tail, helmet head. But a skeleton scan showed no bony crown on its head.
Then the DNA came back. It isn't a seahorse at all. It's a whole separate group, sitting on the branch right next to them.
Scientists named three species in October 2026. Their nickname is sea muppets. Which means nature invented the seahorse shape at least twice.
None has turned up in nearly twenty years. That's why only seven of these fish were ever found.
